title: Short Track Glove Tips and Cut Resistant Gloves: A Complete Guide for Skaters
thumbnail_text: Is your glove costing you speed in corners?

scenes.heading: Short Track Glove Tips and Cut Resistant Gloves
scenes.sub: Faster corners and safer hands, from tip choice to replacement
scenes.narration: This guide shows you how glove tips help you hold speed through the corner, and how a cut resistant glove protects your hand when things go wrong. You will learn how to choose tips, where to fit them, how to size your gloves, and when to replace them. Gloves get the least attention of any short track kit, and the most abuse. Skaters obsess over blades and boots. Then they drag one hand along the ice at forty kilometres per hour, lap after lap, on a glove they bought two seasons ago. That hand is not decoration. It is a reference point and a balance aid, and on a tight radius it is part of how you hold a line.

scenes.heading: Why the hand touches the ice
bullets: Not support, and not a crutch
A light sensor on the ice
Confirms your lean angle
Gives your brain a fixed reference
scenes.chapter: Why the hand touches the ice
scenes.narration: Many new skaters think the hand down is for support. It should not be. You are not leaning on the ice. On a well ridden corner, your hand is a light sensor. It tells you where the ice is. It confirms your lean angle. And it gives your brain a fixed point of reference while your body does something quite unnatural at speed. So what you want from that hand is consistency. It should slide the same way every lap and send you the same feedback. It should never suddenly grab or catch. A tip that grips when you do not expect it does more than scrub speed. It can pull your shoulder, break your line, and put you into the pads.

Here is a skater leaning through a corner. The blue line is the body, tilted away from the vertical. The orange arc marks the lean angle. The green dot is the inside hand, resting lightly on the ice. Along the bottom, the orange arrow shows drag on the hand, and that drag slows you down. The panel on the right lists what a glove tip changes. You get a smooth, hard contact face. You get the same feel on lap one and on lap ten. And you get no sudden grab or catch. Bare fabric gives you none of this.

scenes.heading: The friction problem
bullets: Bare fabric gets wet and freezes
It wears through in a few sessions
Drag changes from lap to lap
Tips give hard, smooth, low friction contact
scenes.narration: Bare fabric on ice is unpredictable. It gets wet. It freezes. It wears through in a few sessions. And the amount of drag changes from your first lap to your last, as the fabric picks up moisture and ice crystals. Glove tips fix this. They put a hard, smooth, low friction surface between your fingers and the ice. That is the whole job of a tip. Less drag. More predictability. More speed carried through the apex, instead of bleeding it away every time your fingers make contact. You can skate without tips, and beginners often do. Most skaters fit them as soon as they are putting a hand down consistently.

scenes.heading: Solid colour or carbon fibre tips
bullets: Solid colour: the sensible default
Five colours to match your club kit
Carbon fibre: stiff, light and tough
Higher volume skaters gain the most
scenes.narration: The guide compares two families of StayBent Quick Tips. The solid colour version is the sensible default for most skaters. It comes in five colours: red, green, blue, black and white. It does the core job without complication, and it is the cheaper way in. That matters while you are still learning where your hand lands. The carbon fibre version uses a carbon weave set in strong, durable resin. Carbon is stiff for its weight, so the tip holds its shape and its surface under load. Which one suits you depends on volume. If you train corners several times a week, or you are hard on kit, carbon earns its place because you replace it less often. If you skate twice a week and your tips last a season, solid colour is the better value.

scenes.heading: Which fingers need tips
bullets: Fit tips only where you touch
Your wear pattern tells the truth
Two scuffed fingers, two tips
No wear? Fix the technique first
scenes.narration: How many tips you need is personal, and worth testing. Many skaters only fit tips to the fingers that actually make contact, usually the ones on the outside edge of the hand. Look at your own gloves. The wear pattern tells you the truth about your hand position better than any coach at the boards. If only two fingers are scuffed, that is where your tips belong. If nothing is scuffed at all, that tells you something too. Either you are not putting a hand down consistently yet, or you press hard on one or two laps and float the rest. Fix the technique first. Then buy tips to support it. And on a standard oval, the inside hand is your left. Fit that glove first.

scenes.heading: Cut resistant, not cut proof
bullets: Tips handle the corner
Cut resistant fabric handles the crash
Hands sit close to other blades
No glove makes a blade harmless
scenes.narration: Tips handle the corner. Cut resistant fabric handles the crash. Short track puts several skaters on a small radius with sharpened steel on their feet. Your hands are low, forward, and close to other people's blades. That is simply the geometry of the sport. A cut resistant glove adds a protective layer for that moment. But be clear about one thing. Cut resistant does not mean cut proof. These fabrics are designed to resist a blade and slow it, so a very serious cut becomes something far less serious. No glove makes a sharpened blade harmless. So wear the protection, and also skate aware of where other people's feet are. You need both. Protective rules vary by event, so check the rules for each competition you enter.

This diagram shows a glove from above. The two fingers marked in green are the ones that usually touch the ice. Your own wear pattern decides this, not the shape of the glove. On the right are four fit checks to run before every season. The glove should be snug across the palm, knuckle to knuckle. Your fingertips should reach the end without bunching. There should be no loose fabric to pinch on the back of the hand. And the glove should not rotate when you twist it. A loose glove moves your tips away from where you fitted them. If you fall between sizes, take the smaller one if the glove stretches, or the larger one if you wear a thin liner underneath.

scenes.heading: Fitting your tips properly
bullets: Clean and fully dry the fingertips
Mark where your hand really touches
Give the adhesive its full cure
Fit a week before a race, then train
scenes.narration: Fitting is where most people rush, then wonder why their tips fall off mid session. Take ten careful minutes. First, clean and dry. Adhesive and epoxy both hate moisture and grease. Wipe the fingertips and let them dry fully. Second, mark before you commit. Put the glove on, get into your hand down position, and see where contact really happens. Fit the tips there, not where the glove pattern suggests. Third, cure properly. Give the adhesive the full cure time the maker specifies, at room temperature, undisturbed. Never fit tips the night before a competition. Do it a week out, then train in them. If tips keep coming off, it is almost always one of these three steps.

scenes.heading: Care and when to replace
bullets: Air dry after every session
Keep gloves away from heaters
Check tips for roughness and lifting
Replace on condition, not calendar
scenes.narration: Gloves come off the ice wet. Left in a bag, they smell, the fabric degrades, and the adhesive bond suffers. Take them out, open them up, and let them air dry at room temperature. Keep them away from heaters, because heat softens adhesive and warps composite parts. In a humid Indian summer, a fan does more good than any heat source. Every few sessions, run a finger over each tip. Check for a rough or scored surface, a worn profile, and any lifting at the edge. A lifting tip will come off at the worst moment. On the glove, look for thinning or an opened weave. There is no set lap count. Replace on condition, never on calendar. And after any big blade change, check your wear pattern again.

scenes.heading: Your inside hand is a sensor. Give it a smooth, safe surface.
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Here is the short version. Your hands do real work in short track. Give them low friction tips so the corner behaves the way you expect. Put cut resistant fabric between your skin and other people's steel. Size everything snug. Dry it after every session. And replace it on condition, not on hope. The full guide is on the LiveLica blog, with more detail on choosing tips, sizing, fitting and care. The link is in the description.
